cards.source_title: Open sourcing HumanLayer
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: software factories have to be open and composable.
cards.claim: Software factories should be assembled from the team's own compute, harnesses and review flows, not bought as a black box in the middle of the SDLC.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated as a belief; he says every team they talk to builds their own.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious; supports keeping the FixFlow harness as owned, composable workflow files

cards.source_title: Open sourcing HumanLayer
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: closed source tools become frustrating because you can't fix them
cards.claim: Dex endorses David Crawshaw's argument that once the agent can read and patch the source of its tools, closed-source tools are a liability because you cannot fix or customize them.
cards.evidence_detail: Attributed to Crawshaw's 'Devtools must be open source'; no data.
cards.landing: tool choice for the harness: prefer tools the agent can read and patch; nowhere specific in FixFlow

cards.source_title: Open sourcing HumanLayer
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: walk me through getting the devstack up and running
cards.claim: Setup documentation can be replaced by a one-line prompt asking a coding agent to walk the user through bringing up the stack.
cards.evidence_detail: Offered as the instruction for self-hosting; no outcome data. Also lists the bundled 'RPI skills and the Linear CLI' as open source.
cards.landing: cold-resume trial / onboarding: a repo that an agent can set up from the repo alone

cards.source_title: show-me: a coding agent skill for compact visual representations
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: agents got more intelligent on paper, but the experience of using them got noticeably worse
cards.claim: Current coding agents answer in walls of jargon that are hard to read, and this happens multiple times a day even with newer models.
cards.evidence_detail: Cites tweets from Yishan, Mario Zechner and Connor from Replicas, plus his own frequent experience; no numbers.
cards.landing: agent output style: owner-view and closing-message readability; a skill or CLAUDE.md output rule

cards.source_title: show-me: a coding agent skill for compact visual representations
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Restate your last message. Stop using jargon and speak coherently.
cards.claim: A tiny restate-in-plain-language skill (Dillon Mulroy's /bro) is a cheap fix for unreadable agent replies; the full text is two sentences.
cards.evidence_detail: Skill contents quoted in full; no measurement.
cards.landing: a small skill under .claude/skills/ for restating a message plainly

cards.source_title: show-me: a coding agent skill for compact visual representations
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: your visual cortex was trained over millions of years to process rich visual information effortlessly
cards.claim: Design the agent's communication for the human visual system (after Coda Hale): analysing prose is exhausting, so optimise tools to fit the human mind.
cards.evidence_detail: Principle borrowed from Coda Hale's talk on intuition vs. attention; no data.
cards.landing: phase closing message and one-page owner view: prefer diagrams, trees, tables over prose

cards.source_title: show-me: a coding agent skill for compact visual representations
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: You should be discussing the shape of the code
cards.claim: Program design (types, signatures, call stacks) should be discussed with the human before agents write code; it is the phase many people now skip but is essential.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated opinion; show-me is offered as the tool for this.
cards.landing: phase routine: a design/shape review step before the draft PR's implementation; plan PR body

cards.source_title: show-me: a coding agent skill for compact visual representations
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: explore large diffs post-hoc to understand what to dig into during review
cards.claim: The same compact visual forms can be used after the fact to navigate a large diff and decide where a human reviewer should dig.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated use; no example numbers.
cards.landing: Opus reviewer per PR / owner view: a visual outline of the diff

cards.source_title: show-me: a coding agent skill for compact visual representations
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: A shallow file tree, one line of responsibility per entry.
cards.claim: A catalogue of compact forms (component trees, call stacks, file layouts with one-line responsibilities, pseudocode, types and signatures, and +/- diff syntax over trees and call stacks) replaces prose when explaining or proposing a change.
cards.evidence_detail: Worked examples given for each form; no measurements.
cards.landing: a show-me-like skill; plan PR body format for backend slice changes

cards.source_title: show-me: a coding agent skill for compact visual representations
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: tanish even wrote a tool to compute them straight from the AST
cards.claim: Call stacks can be computed deterministically from the AST by a tool rather than written by the model; Dex points to this as a way to produce the call-stack view.
cards.evidence_detail: Links a third-party tool (Tanishq) with no evaluation. Re-opens the call-graph tooling the harness review skipped.
cards.landing: call-graph tooling (previously skipped by the harness review); would feed program-design and review steps

cards.source_title: show-me: a coding agent skill for compact visual representations
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we like state diagrams and sequence diagrams the most
cards.claim: Inline mermaid state and sequence diagrams help when the chat UI renders them, though they are sometimes still slop.
cards.evidence_detail: Preference stated; he admits they are 'usually better than reading words' but not always good.
cards.landing: job lifecycle state machine and outbox flows in docs; plan PR body

cards.source_title: show-me: a coding agent skill for compact visual representations
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: HTML has replaced figma for a lot of our prototyping work.
cards.claim: HumanLayer uses agent-generated HTML for mockups and explainers (and lets the agent embed HTML in replies) instead of design tools; show-me is billed as lighter and faster than HTML for most dev problems.
cards.evidence_detail: Team practice; no numbers.
cards.landing: owner view as an HTML explainer rather than markdown

cards.source_title: show-me: a coding agent skill for compact visual representations
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: npx skills add humanlayer/skills --skill show-me
cards.claim: Skills are distributed as installable packages from a shared skills repo (npx skills add), and invoked as /show-me or by asking; user can say 'this is too much content. show me.'
cards.evidence_detail: Install and usage instructions; asks users to tweet results.
cards.landing: skill distribution: .claude/skills/ checked in; a reusable workflow library

cards.source_title: /show-me: compact visual representations for coding agents (X article)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the thing people used to love about claude - its voice, it's personality, its "soul" has been flushed out in the RL dungeon
cards.claim: Dex asserts that RL post-training stripped the model's voice and personality, making agent output harder to read.
cards.evidence_detail: Opinion; the blog version has the same sentence. The X article also says the built-in HumanLayer version has inline HTML and diagrams first-class and credits a skill originally from @backnotprop.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious

cards.source_title: Getting Claude to Actually Read Your CLAUDE.md
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: explicitly tells the model the contents "may or may not be relevant."
cards.claim: Claude Code wraps CLAUDE.md in a system-reminder saying the contents may not be relevant, so the longer the file, the more sections the model treats as optional.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated as observed behaviour of the harness; no measurement.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md: explains why length hurts adherence; supports the gated trim

cards.source_title: Getting Claude to Actually Read Your CLAUDE.md
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: <important if="you are writing or modifying tests">
cards.claim: Wrapping domain-specific CLAUDE.md sections in <important if="condition"> blocks gives noticeably better adherence on tasks where only some sections apply.
cards.evidence_detail: 'We don't have a rigorous explanation'; his guess is the explicit condition signals relevance. No numbers.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md: wrap the mobile-outbox, dispatcher, bill-freeze and migration invariants in conditional blocks

cards.source_title: Getting Claude to Actually Read Your CLAUDE.md
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: The conditional blocks are for testing setup or deployment procedures that only matter sometimes.
cards.claim: Do not wrap everything: project identity, directory structure and tech stack stay unconditional, and each condition must be narrow ('you are writing code' matches almost everything and defeats the purpose).
cards.evidence_detail: Rules of thumb from his own use.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md trim: keep stack table unconditional, conditionalise the invariants by task type

cards.source_title: Getting Claude to Actually Read Your CLAUDE.md
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: stale code snippets, style rules that should be in a linter, vague instructions
cards.claim: An improve-claude-md skill automates restructuring a CLAUDE.md: extracts foundational content, wraps the rest in conditions, and removes stale snippets, linter-able style rules and vague instructions; output should still be reviewed.
cards.evidence_detail: Skill description; he says 'it's not perfect'.
cards.landing: the CLAUDE.md trim: run or copy this skill as a first pass (gated behind the knowledge-store pilot)

cards.source_title: Long-Context Isn't the Answer
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: instruction adherence was dramatically degraded, and not just at longer context lengths
cards.claim: After a couple of weeks with Opus 4.6 (1M context) HumanLayer saw worse instruction adherence even within the 200k range (ignoring design docs, trivial mistakes, disobeying) and switched back to Opus 4.5.
cards.evidence_detail: Weeks of team use; no benchmark numbers.
cards.landing: model/effort routing: do not assume a bigger-window model follows instructions better; pin verifier model by evidence

cards.source_title: Long-Context Isn't the Answer
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: how many instructions they can follow reasonably well before instruction adherence drops off
cards.claim: There is a measurable per-model 'instruction budget' that correlates with model size, and extended-context variants (YaRN-style) get a bigger window but the same budget.
cards.evidence_detail: Refers to an earlier study (chart not visible); the YaRN claim is stated as 'likely'.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md length target; phase routine: cap instructions loaded per phase

cards.source_title: Long-Context Isn't the Answer
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: digging us deeper into the dumb zone
cards.claim: Treat the context window as a haystack in which every CLAUDE.md line, tool description, tool result and message competes; a bigger haystack with the same needle makes finding the relevant instruction harder.
cards.evidence_detail: Analogy, no numbers.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md trim; one phase per new session

cards.source_title: Long-Context Isn't the Answer
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: All non-trivial operations should be delegated to sub-agents.
cards.claim: A 'subagent-orchestrator' skill tells the parent to delegate research, codebase understanding and verbose bash/gh/aws investigation to sub-agents, use one sub-agent per distinct task, and not split overlapping tasks; it kept Opus coherent at longer context.
cards.evidence_detail: Skill text printed in full; reports it helped 'in combination with our existing workflow skills'; no numbers.
cards.landing: an orchestrator skill in .claude/skills/; sub-agent delegation for log/CI digging

cards.source_title: Long-Context Isn't the Answer
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: trigger at the 100k token mark instead of 40% of the usable context
cards.claim: HumanLayer's context-high warning was moved from ~40% of Sonnet's 168k usable window (~100k tokens) to a flat 100k tokens for long-context models, which is only 10% of Opus 1M.
cards.evidence_detail: Concrete thresholds: 168k = 200k minus 32k output reserve; 40% about 100k; 10% of 1M.
cards.landing: phase routine: a ~100k-token wrap-up trigger inside a phase; context budget check (the harness review skipped a context system)

cards.source_title: Long-Context Isn't the Answer
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: Context isolation beats context expansion.
cards.claim: Keep each window small and focused via sub-agents, progressive disclosure and context-efficient backpressure rather than a larger window; long-context models degrade at all lengths, not just long ones.
cards.evidence_detail: TL;DR of the post; supported only by the team's experience.
cards.landing: validates one-phase-per-new-session; sub-agent use inside phases

cards.source_title: Context Forking to Save Time, Tokens and Trouble
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: the context window only lets you push or pop from the newest end
cards.claim: Model the context window as a downward-growing stack: you can pop whole user-message turns but not edit the middle, because random access causes cache misses, mangles context and breaks the harness's read-before-edit state.
cards.evidence_detail: Conceptual model with three stated reasons; no measurement.
cards.landing: compaction and context budget: why editing history is not an option; rewind instead

cards.source_title: Context Forking to Save Time, Tokens and Trouble
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: I'll fork the conversation to explore different design & architectural paths.
cards.claim: Build high-quality codebase context once, then fork the session several times to explore alternative designs, review the results and pick one or decide more research is needed.
cards.evidence_detail: Author's own habit in the design phase.
cards.landing: phase routine: fork from a warmed research session for alternative plans; judge-panel inputs

cards.source_title: Context Forking to Save Time, Tokens and Trouble
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: reads all 40,000 tokens one chunk at a time
cards.claim: When the agent floods context with a huge file or command output (the 40,000-token example), rewind to before it rather than continuing in a polluted window; harnesses often guard this by writing output to a file and showing the path.
cards.evidence_detail: One example number (40,000 tokens); no experiment.
cards.landing: output backpressure: output-to-file guards; rewind instead of compaction after a context blow-up

cards.source_title: Context Forking to Save Time, Tokens and Trouble
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: Rewinding to course-correct an agent
cards.claim: If the agent missed something mid-implementation, rewind to the turn boundary before it and re-steer rather than appending a correction to a long history.
cards.evidence_detail: Listed use case with a diagram; no data.
cards.landing: phase routine: course-correct by rewinding rather than piling on corrections

cards.source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: it's not a model problem. It's a configuration problem
cards.claim: Agent failures across dozens of projects and hundreds of sessions are mostly harness configuration problems, and smarter models will only be given harder tasks and keep failing in unexpected ways.
cards.evidence_detail: 'Dozens of projects and hundreds of agent sessions'; no counts of failures.
cards.landing: frames the whole harness review: fix the harness, not wait for models

cards.source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: anytime you find an agent makes a mistake, you take the time to engineer
cards.claim: Adopting Mitchell Hashimoto's definition: every observed agent mistake gets a solution engineered so it never recurs; but they do not hunt for problems preemptively.
cards.evidence_detail: Quote from Hashimoto, endorsed; the post's closing notes add 'bias towards shipping'.
cards.landing: phase routine decisions journal and register of failures; every closing message names a harness fix

cards.source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: hooks for automated integration and deterministic control flow
cards.claim: Beyond Viv's four levers, add hooks (deterministic control flow) and skills (progressive disclosure; Dex calls them 'Instruction Modules') as harness levers; harness engineering is a subset of context engineering.
cards.evidence_detail: Conceptual framing.
cards.landing: hooks (previously skipped) as the deterministic complement to CLAUDE.md prose

cards.source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: Sub-agents function as a "context firewall"
cards.claim: Sub-agents are the key to coherence over many sessions because only the prompt and the final result enter the parent context; none of the intermediate tool calls do.
cards.evidence_detail: Months of brownfield enterprise-scale work; no numbers.
cards.landing: sub-agents for research/locator tasks (extends the Haiku fixflow-explorer)

cards.source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: It doesn't work. What does work is using sub-agents for context control.
cards.claim: Role-persona sub-agents (frontend engineer, backend engineer, data analyst) do not work; sub-agents are for context control, not specialisation by job title.
cards.evidence_detail: Tried and abandoned; no numbers. A claim against a common pattern.
cards.landing: custom agents: define them by task shape (locate, analyse, trace), not by persona

cards.source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: no need to burn Opus tokens on a codebase grep
cards.claim: Use an expensive model (Opus) for the parent that plans and orchestrates, and Sonnet or Haiku for sub-agents that get small discrete tasks.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated practice; no cost figures.
cards.landing: effort/model routing: Haiku for locators (already), Sonnet for readers, Opus only for judge/verify

cards.source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: cite sources in filepath:line format or with URLs
cards.claim: Sub-agents should return a condensed answer plus filepath:line or URL citations, so the parent sees the answer but can follow up (progressive disclosure of evidence).
cards.evidence_detail: Their own sub-agent format.
cards.landing: fixflow-explorer output contract; verifier reports citing file:line

cards.source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: what should it do, but also what should it not do
cards.claim: A sub-agent system prompt must specify role scope (including what not to do), what to return and in what form, and which tools it has; the loose-scope alternative produces a game of telephone when sub-agents dispatch sub-agents via MCP.
cards.evidence_detail: Checklist of three items; the telephone warning is a joke illustration.
cards.landing: agent file template for .claude/agents/

cards.source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: Trying to micro-optimize which sub-agents could access which tools.
cards.claim: Restricting per-sub-agent tool access finely led to tool thrash and worse results, so do not spend effort on it.
cards.evidence_detail: Listed under 'what didn't work'.
cards.landing: custom agent tool lists: keep coarse

cards.source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: LLM-generated ones actually hurt performance while costing 20%+ more
cards.claim: Summarising the ETH Zurich study of 138 agent files: LLM-generated agent files hurt and cost 20%+ more, human-written ones helped only ~4%, agents spent 14-22% more reasoning tokens, and codebase overviews and directory listings did not help.
cards.evidence_detail: Third-party study (138 agentfiles, various repos) as summarised by Kyle; he argues it confirms their earlier advice.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md trim: the stack table and 'where things live' directory listings are the content the study found useless

cards.source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: Our CLAUDE.md is under 60 lines.
cards.claim: HumanLayer's own CLAUDE.md is under 60 lines, kept concise and universally applicable, with as few instructions as reasonably possible and progressive disclosure for the rest.
cards.evidence_detail: A single stated number; FixFlow's file is about 390 lines.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md length target

cards.source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: never connect to one you don't trust
cards.claim: MCP tool descriptions land in the system prompt, so an untrusted MCP server is a prompt-injection vector (and stdio servers can run code); too many tools also burn context and instruction budget, so switch off unused servers.
cards.evidence_detail: Warning plus reference to Anthropic's MCP tool search; no numbers.
cards.landing: MCP/tool hygiene in .claude settings

cards.source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: This saved us thousands of tokens from the MCP server's tool definitions
cards.claim: Replace a broad MCP server with a small purpose-built CLI wrapper with context-efficient output, and put about six example usages in CLAUDE.md; where a well-trained CLI already exists (gh, docker, DB clients) just prompt for the CLI.
cards.evidence_detail: Linear CLI example, 'thousands of tokens' saved, no exact count.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md or skill examples for repo scripts; small CLIs for CI and Railway reads

cards.source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: the agent only gets access to specific instructions, knowledge, or tools when it decides
cards.claim: Skills fix the instruction-budget problem through progressive disclosure: SKILL.md loads as a user message on activation, and a skill can bundle further markdown files and CLIs that SKILL.md points to conditionally.
cards.evidence_detail: 'We kept stuffing every instruction and tool into the system prompt, and the agent kept getting worse.'
cards.landing: move task-specific CLAUDE.md invariants into skills with bundled reference files

cards.source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: Treat skills like you'd treat npm install random-package
cards.claim: Skill registries have distributed hundreds of malicious skills; read any skill before installing since skills can run arbitrary code.
cards.evidence_detail: Links a report; 'hundreds' is quoted from it, not counted by the author.
cards.landing: policy for importing third-party skills (e.g. show-me, improve-claude-md): read before adopting

cards.source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: exit code 2 tells the harness to re-engage the agent
cards.claim: A Stop hook that runs formatter and typecheck, is silent on success, and exits 2 with only the errors on failure forces the agent to keep working until the checks pass; requires typecheck/build in a handful of seconds.
cards.evidence_detail: Full bash script shown from their repo; no result numbers.
cards.landing: hooks (previously skipped): Stop hook running ruff/mypy/tsc quickly; marks a re-opened skip

cards.source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: we automatically deny any Bash() tool calls that try to run migrations
cards.claim: Hooks can auto-approve or deny tool calls on input values with more expressive rules than default permissions, e.g. deny Bash migration commands with an instruction to ask the user to run them; also used for notifications, Slack/PR integrations and a coverage-drop Stop hook.
cards.evidence_detail: Examples of their own hook uses.
cards.landing: hooks (previously skipped): a PreToolUse guard for alembic/railway up from repo root; coverage Stop hook

cards.source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: strongly correlated with the agent's ability to verify its own work
cards.claim: The likelihood of solving a problem with a coding agent correlates strongly with the agent's ability to verify its own work, so typechecks, tests, coverage and UI tests are among the highest-leverage investments.
cards.evidence_detail: Experience claim; no data.
cards.landing: verifiers and backpressure; fail-before/pass-after requirement

cards.source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: 4,000 lines of passing tests would flood the context window
cards.claim: Verification output must be context-efficient: running the whole suite after every change dumped 4,000 lines of passing tests and the agent started hallucinating about test files, so swallow output and surface only errors (success silent).
cards.evidence_detail: One failure story with a line count.
cards.landing: output caps on CI/test commands used by agents; a run-silent wrapper

cards.source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: Running our entire test suite (5+ minutes) at the end of every agent session
cards.claim: Running the full 5+ minute suite at the end of every session did not work; run a relevant subset instead.
cards.evidence_detail: Listed under what didn't work.
cards.landing: phase routine test selection; stop-hook scope

cards.source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: Starting simple and adding configuration only when the agent actually failed
cards.claim: What worked: start simple, add config only after real failures, throw away what does not help (many more hooks discarded than kept), distribute tested config to the team via the repo, optimise iteration speed over one-shot success. What did not: designing the ideal harness upfront, installing dozens of skills and MCP servers 'just in case'.
cards.evidence_detail: Author's retrospective; no numbers.
cards.landing: how to grow the skill and agent set: failure-driven, prune; repo-level config

cards.source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: models can be over-fitted to their harness
cards.claim: Models are post-trained on their own harness, but can also be over-fitted to it: citing Viv, Opus 4.6 ranks #33 on Terminal Bench 2.0 in Claude Code and #5 in an unseen harness.
cards.evidence_detail: Terminal Bench 2.0 positions (#33 vs #5, +/- ~4) via a third-party post.
cards.landing: argues for harness customisation rather than defaults; evidence for model-vs-harness effects

cards.source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: performance degrades as context length increases — even on simple tasks
cards.claim: Chroma's context-rot study (18 models, needle-in-haystack) shows degradation with length even on simple tasks, steeper when the question and the relevant text have low semantic similarity; irrelevant tool results act as distractors that compound.
cards.evidence_detail: Third-party study of 18 models; he notes it differs from agentic coding.
cards.landing: supports one phase per session and sub-agent isolation; CLAUDE.md distractor risk

cards.source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: an unpredictable game of telephone
cards.claim: For harnesses without sub-agents, an MCP server that launches a fresh agent session and returns its final message can emulate sub-agents; beware nested dispatch and raise the MCP timeout.
cards.evidence_detail: A 'very rough approximation' linked; caveats stated.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious; relevant only if other agent runtimes are used

cards.source_title: A Brief History of Ralph
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: while : ; do cat PROMPT.md | npx --yes @sourcegraph/amp ; done
cards.claim: The core of ralph is a one-line bash loop feeding the same prompt file to an agent repeatedly; Dex keeps using '5-line bash loops'.
cards.evidence_detail: Geoff Huntley's July 2025 post as reproduced by Dex; Dex says he is still using bash loops.
cards.landing: unattended loop pattern; simplest possible saved workflow

cards.source_title: A Brief History of Ralph
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: carve off small bits of work into independent context windows
cards.claim: The key point of ralph is not running forever but carving small units of work into independent context windows.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex's reading, used to criticise the Anthropic plugin.
cards.landing: validates one phase per new session and small work units

cards.source_title: A Brief History of Ralph
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: adds an opaque stop hook for all claude sessions in a directory
cards.claim: Criticism of Anthropic's official ralph-wiggum plugin: it dies cryptically without --dangerously-skip-permissions, installs hooks in places you cannot find, tracks state in a strange markdown file, adds an opaque stop hook to every session in the directory until disabled, can break claude in the repo if the state file is deleted first, and misses the point of ralph.
cards.evidence_detail: His own test in Dec 2025, retried in the Jan 1 2026 showdown; no numbers.
cards.landing: hooks (previously skipped): any hook must be visible, in-repo and removable; against opaque state files

cards.source_title: A Brief History of Ralph
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if the specs are bad, the results will be meh
cards.claim: A GTD-app experiment where one ralph wrote specs and another built from them, with neither specs nor code read, produced poor output; lessons: bad specs mean meh results, know your end-state workflows and how you will test them, and do not use ralph when exploring.
cards.evidence_detail: One Saturday-morning toy project.
cards.landing: phase routine: human reads the spec/plan before implementation; do not loop without a testable end state

cards.source_title: A Brief History of Ralph
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: code is cheap - the easier alternative to "merge/rebase" is just to re-run the ralph loop
cards.claim: In a React refactor ralph ran about 6 hours after ~1 hour of writing a standards doc (30 min with Claude, 30 min with an experienced engineer); the PR hit merge conflicts and was never merged, so the lesson is to re-run the loop on fresh code rather than rebase.
cards.evidence_detail: Timings: 30 + 30 min spec, 6 h loop; PR closed unmerged.
cards.landing: large mechanical refactors: re-run rather than rebase; human-refined standards doc as the spec

cards.source_title: A Brief History of Ralph
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Waking up to one small refactor every morning is better than both
cards.claim: For existing codebases, run ralph-ish desired-state loops once per night on a cron and merge small iterations over time, rather than one giant diff or none.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated as the team's practice after the refactor experiment.
cards.landing: scheduled overnight single-iteration workflows for tech debt; keep change set reviewable
